source.author: Lisa J. Dettling
source.title: Broadband in the Labor Market: The Impact of Residential High-Speed Internet on Married Women’s Labor Force Participation
source.version: February 2015 working paper; not verified identical to ILR Review 2017 journal version
source.locator: Table 3 column 5, printed page 39; explanation printed page 17

population: CPS adults 18–59; August 2000, September 2001, October 2003, 2007 and 2009 supplements; state-level instrument, not county introduction
treatment: Individual self-reported home high-speed Internet use; instrumented by state multiple-dwelling-unit share interacted with survey year

identifiedContrast.kind: Married women versus pooled single women/men using high-speed Internet
identifiedContrast.rangeMethod: Calculated normal approximation coefficient ±1.96 reported clustered SE; not a source-printed interval; Team9 verification requested

absoluteMarriedWomenEffect.exactMissingFigure: Covariance of main HSI and married-interaction estimates in Table3 column5 (or reported SE/CI for their sum). Do not apply interaction SE to the 4.1pp sum.

activation.operation: hold existing absolute-participation link pending correct interval and dimensional bridge
activation.reason: Current link targets absolute married-women participation, not subgroup contrast. Engine treats size as proportional response per cause unit; the source estimates a probability-point change for binary adoption. A place share percentage point is not one household adoption.

why: Home broadband can enable telework or reduce time spent on home production.
A person with actual access and a usable work arrangement can fit paid work around household responsibilities.
The author finds a heterogeneous labor-supply response for married women; the paper does not turn a broadband appropriation into employment.
The chain reaches a researched decision mechanism, but this game lacks the household-adoption, work-arrangement and time-budget bridge for this link.
conditions: Applies to the studied adult population and early broadband diffusion, not all 2026 households or a universal county effect.
Education and children vary the response; some subgroup first stages are marginally weak.
Access, actual home use, telework opportunity and care obligations are distinct records.
reverseOnRepeal: Repealing public provision does not automatically remove an existing subscription, private service or telework job; no symmetric reversal estimate is established.
who: Married women in the studied adult sample, with comparison groups specified; no named saved person is claimed affected.
lagWhy: A survey-based diffusion comparison supplies no zero-month response estimate for a new local government program.
personReader: No person feels this yet from the current null aggregate link; a source contrast is not a recorded hiring or participation decision.
